correctness.rationale: The Laplace transform of radius-R integrals equals 16s³/prod(s²+4pi²k_j²). Integer phases e^(±2pi ia)=1 permit paired-pole cancellation, and only a triple zero or triple/quadruple repeated nonzero |k_j| can contribute a third-order principal part, yielding the stated coefficient cases. Independent direct 1D slice integration gave Fourier coefficients (0,0,0,1)=2/pi² and (0,0,0,2)=1/(2pi²). A separate four-fold combinatorial enumeration of all k in [-N,N]^4 for N=0,1,2,3 returned 1,57,241,553 as predicted. Fourier uniqueness and order-minus-two homogeneity yield all integer-m scaling. The lattice nearest-neighbor graph is bipartite, precluding triple overlaps, and eight unit-neighbor pairs have individual overlap volume 1/24, so a 1/6 double-cover fraction, 1/3 single-cover and 1/2 zero-cover fraction follow from average volume 2/3. Higher repeated-pole cases follow the reviewed exact algebra rather than finite sampling.

originality.rationale: Best-of-knowledge originality of the exact final combined claim, after reviewing primary statements and Resultary hits; credited known partial antecedents. The 4D unit-axis cross-polytope is a rational equal-axis specialization of general algebraic cross-polytopes, but Fourier coefficient support at integer frequencies and periodized overlap-level distribution are different from counting lattice points in dilates. Borda Theorem 3 gives a general simplex contour transform and covers high-order pole techniques after triangulation. This is a computational route to the claimed Fourier coefficients, not a stated classification of 4D integer repeated-frequency cancellations and exact three nonconstant coverage levels. Borda Proposition 4 imposes algebraically independent reciprocal-axis hypotheses inapplicable to all equal axes. General Fourier contour and Poisson summation identities do not alone assert the sparse support count or all-m multiplicity distribution. Gravin–Robins–Shiryaev classifies constant translation multiplicities; the present periodization is manifestly nonconstant at m=1, so a constant-tiling theorem does not imply it.
